opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a while thinking about. At first glance they look like separate problems. Speculative decoding is an inference-time trick: you have a small, cheap draft model that proposes a few tokens, and the big target model verifies them in parallel. Distillation is a training-time thing, where you're trying to compress a big teacher into a smaller student. But the connection is very direct once you look at what actually makes speculative decoding fast.

The speedup depends almost entirely on the acceptance rate, meaning how often the target model agrees with what the draft model proposed. And the acceptance rate is a function of how close the draft model's distribution is to the target's. Specifically, it's tied to the total variation distance between the two distributions. So if you want a better draft model, what you really want is a draft model that's well *aligned* with the target. That is exactly a distillation problem: train the small model to match the big one.

The interesting part is that the details matter a lot. A few things fell out of thinking about it this way.

First, which data you distill on. In speculative decoding, the draft model generates the tokens, and then the target checks them. So the draft model is being evaluated on its *own* generations. That argues strongly for on-policy distillation, where you sample from the student and have the teacher give feedback on those samples, rather than just training on a fixed dataset or on teacher outputs. Training on teacher-generated sequences gives you this train-test mismatch, a kind of exposure bias, because at inference the student goes off into its own regions of the space. On-policy data fixes that.

Second, which divergence you minimize. People default to forward KL, but there's no reason that's optimal here. Forward KL, reverse KL, Jensen-Shannon, total variation. They behave differently, for example mode-covering versus mode-seeking. And the best choice actually depends on the task and the decoding strategy, whether you're doing greedy or sampling at some temperature. Since the acceptance rate is literally tied to total variation distance, you can even optimize something close to the thing you care about directly.

Third, the nice thing about speculative decoding is that the output distribution is guaranteed to be the target model's distribution. It's lossless. So distillation in this setting is a pure latency win. You're not trading off quality like you usually are when you deploy a distilled model. A better-aligned draft just means more accepted tokens per verification step, which means faster wall-clock generation.

And you can push it further. If you're willing to relax the losslessness a bit, using lenient acceptance criteria, you get a whole quality-latency tradeoff curve, and distillation shifts that whole curve in your favor.

So the way I'd summarize it: speculative decoding tells you *what objective* your small model should be trained for, which is alignment with the target on the student's own outputs, and distillation, especially on-policy distillation, is the tool for getting there. It's a nice case where thinking about the inference setup tells you how to do the training properly.

r001.rationale: The response says the target model verifies tokens proposed by the draft and describes on-policy distillation as having the teacher give feedback on the draft model’s own samples.

r002.rationale: It contrasts target verification with teacher feedback, but does not mention logits or distinguish logit-level feedback from accepting or rejecting a proposed sequence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of my favorite connections, because on the surface they look like completely different problems. Speculative decoding is a systems trick for making inference faster, and distillation is a training recipe for making a small model good. But if you look at what you actually need for speculative decoding to work well, it's the same thing distillation is trying to give you.

So the setup in speculative decoding is you have a big target model and a small draft model. The draft model proposes a few tokens cheaply, and the big model verifies them in parallel. The whole speedup comes from the acceptance rate, which is how often the big model agrees with what the draft proposed. And that acceptance rate is basically a measure of how close the draft model's distribution is to the target model's distribution. If you write it out, the expected number of accepted tokens is governed by a divergence between the two next-token distributions, something like a total variation distance.

Now, what is distillation? Distillation is literally training a small model to match the distribution of a big model. So the objective you would want to optimize to get a good draft model is a distillation objective. That's the connection. The draft model is a student, the target model is the teacher, and the thing you care about at inference time is exactly the thing distillation minimizes.

What's interesting is that once you see it that way, a lot of the knobs in distillation start to matter in ways people didn't appreciate. For example, which divergence you use. Forward KL versus reverse KL versus something in between behaves differently. Reverse KL tends to be mode-seeking, so the student commits to the high-probability modes of the teacher, and that can actually be what you want for acceptance, because you care about the draft being right on the tokens the big model would actually sample. Forward KL is mass-covering, and a student trained that way can spread probability over things the teacher rarely does, which hurts you.

The other knob is the data. Classic distillation uses some fixed dataset. But at inference time the draft model is operating on its own generated prefixes, and then on the big model's corrections. So there's a distribution shift. That's the same problem we ran into with on-policy distillation in general, where you want the student to learn from its own samples with the teacher providing feedback, rather than only from the teacher's samples. For speculative decoding this turns out to be quite natural, because the whole verification step is already generating exactly the data you need. The big model is telling you, at every position, here's what I would have done. So you can do this online. The draft model keeps getting distilled while it's serving, and the acceptance rate just goes up over time, especially for whatever the real traffic distribution looks like.

And the thing I like about it is that it makes the draft model's job very well defined. You're not asking the small model to be a good language model in some general sense. You're asking it to be a good predictor of this one specific big model. That's a narrower, easier target, and distillation is the right tool for hitting it.

r001.rationale: The response frames the target model as a teacher that evaluates the draft model’s proposals and provides feedback about what it would have done at each position.

r002.rationale: It discusses matching the target’s distribution and speculative decoding’s acceptance rate, but does not distinguish fine-grained teacher-logit feedback from accepting or rejecting a proposed sequence.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two ways of using a smaller model to make a larger model’s capabilities cheaper to access. With distillation, you train a smaller model to imitate a larger model, and then you deploy the smaller model on its own. You get efficiency, but potentially give up some quality.

With speculative decoding, the smaller model proposes several tokens, and the larger model verifies them in parallel. With the right acceptance procedure, you preserve the larger model’s output distribution. So the smaller model’s mistakes affect how much speedup you get, rather than the quality of the final output.

The connection is that distillation can give you a better draft model for speculative decoding. But the objective is slightly different: you care about matching the particular model doing the verification, because that determines how many proposed tokens get accepted. And there’s a tradeoff—a more accurate draft model might also be more expensive to run. Ultimately, you want the draft model that gives you the best end-to-end speedup.

r001.rationale: The response says the larger model verifies the smaller model’s proposed tokens, but does not describe that evaluation as teacher feedback.

r002.rationale: It describes acceptance of proposed tokens but does not contrast this with distillation’s fine-grained feedback through teacher logits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two ways of using a smaller model to get some of the benefits of a larger model. With distillation, you’re trying to transfer the larger model’s behavior into the smaller model during training, and then you deploy the smaller model on its own. You get cheaper inference, but you may lose some quality.

With speculative decoding, you keep the larger model in the loop. The smaller model proposes several tokens, and the larger model verifies them in parallel. With the right acceptance procedure, you preserve the larger model’s output distribution while potentially reducing latency.

So distillation can actually help speculative decoding: you can distill the larger model into a draft model that better predicts what it will generate. Better agreement means more accepted tokens and potentially a bigger speedup. The distinction is that the draft model doesn’t have to be a perfect replacement—it just needs to be cheap and agree often enough to make verification worthwhile.

r001.rationale: The response says the larger model verifies the smaller model’s proposed tokens and that distillation can improve the draft model, but it does not characterize that verification as teacher feedback.

r002.rationale: It contrasts training-time distillation with speculative decoding’s acceptance procedure, but does not mention teacher logits or distinguish their fine-grained feedback from sequence-level acceptance or rejection.
